title: Andy's Boogie short and Al Killian's time in the band
summary: Reading from Meeker's film guide, Barnet says he did not play soprano in Andy's Boogie, that Al Killian dominates it, and that Killian played with him in 1941-43 until he was murdered.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Sounds like it would be great. As long as we're on films, may as well go through the book here. David Meeker's, "Jazz in the Movies - A Guide to Jazz Musicians, 1917 to 1977." And these are not chronological, but rather alphabetical. And the first one where you're listed is "Andy's Boogie," 1950, three minutes, Charlie Barnet and his Orchestra in a performance of the title number with the leader soloing on soprano sax. A Snader Telescription. Do you remember that?
That's very interesting, because I recall the arrangement very well, "Andy's Boogie," and I don't play soprano sax on it.
But the arrangement was by Andy Gibson, obviously, and the gentleman who really dominates the whole thing was Al Killian, the trumpet player.
Al played with you when, what years?
Well, Al played with me in, oh, '41, '42. He was -- he left for awhile, and then he came back later in '43, and then he was playing with me when he got murdered out here in California.
He'd just gotten back from Europe with Duke, I know.

That's right, and he had joined my band. I had a band working out of Hollywood, and we were working, and we went up to Bakersfield and played a one nighter, and Al was back with us, and it was that night he got home, and that was when he got -- he was killed.
I remember when he was killed, yeah. Where did you get Al? Was he in another band before he was with your band?
Yeah, he was with Basie, Count Basie, yeah.
He was certainly a phenomenal player.
